mut1gy:276: Goodhart's law plays out starkly in efficiency measurement: once a metric becomes a target, it is no longer a good metric. Lines of code is the most misleading metric in the AI era—the cost of generating redundant code is far lower than manual effort, lines are inflated and positively correlated with maintenance cost; Pass@1 is likewise distorted—it ignores retry cost after failures, and the real cost is the sum of "generation + verification + fixing." Deeper still is the proxy metric disconnect: generation speed, lines per hour, and even CR pass rate are all proxies with no stable correspondence to real outcomes such as defect escape rate and production incidents—AI-written code reviewed by AI creates a closed-loop blind spot, inflating CR pass rates while defects still escape. The way out of the trap is to anchor metrics to "verifiable output"—output that cannot be verified cannot have its quality measured.

vjdi9h:259: Token is a unified unit that connects "speed" and "cost": faster generation means more consumption and real cost. Its value goes beyond accounting; it provides three types of analytical tools. Output association: measure efficiency by "effective output per thousand tokens," binding cost and value in the same unit. Task baseline: establish consumption baselines by task type; abnormal deviation is a diagnostic signal—a small change consuming many tokens with no change in output often means context corruption, retrieval failure, or an infinite loop. Attention budget perspective: the longer the context, the lower the information value per token (attention dilution, "lost in the middle" effect); the token consumption curve can therefore inversely reflect context quality—the key leap that turns cost metrics into quality metrics.
